raw_case_text: A 36-year-old woman was admitted to Imam Khomeini Hospital, Tehran because of acute onset of fever and decreased level of consciousness. Her problem began 3 days prior to admission with hallucination, delusions and fever. She was single and unemployed, living in a small town, without previous history of brucellosis in herself and her family. She was not receiving any medication and had no history of illicit drug use. The only positive point in her past was regular consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. On admission, she had disorientation to time and place. She was agitated and had visual hallucination and grandiose delusion. Despite her high temperature (39 C) other vital signs were normal including blood pressure, pulse rate, and respiratory rate. Head and neck examination revealed nuchal rigidity. General physical examination was normal except for some abnormal neurologic findings including decreased deep tendon reflexes and forces of lower extremities at about 3/5. A lumbar puncture was done after brain computerized tomography scan did not reveal any abnormality. The results of initial tests and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis are listed in table 1. Presence of fever, decreased level of consciousness, and bizarre behavior raised the possibility of herpes simplex virus (HSV) meningoencephalitis, hence intravenous acyclovir started pending further evaluations. Brain MRI with contrast (gadolinium) showed meningeal enhancement in left frontal and right temporal lobes (fig. 1), suggesting meningoencephalitis. During the next few days no significant change was observed in the patient's condition. On the 6th day of hospitalization she developed nausea and vomiting and laboratory tests showed significant elevation of liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, AST = 1,093, and alanine aminotransferase, ALT = 203). Since our patient showed raised levels of liver function tests, we further checked for HBsAg, HCV Ab, HAV Ab (IgM), HIV Ab, EBV Ab (VCA IgM), CMV Ab (IgM), anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, and liver kidney microsomal antibody; all were negative. Because of lack of clinical response to acyclovir therapy, negative CSF HSV PCR results, and possibility of drug-induced hepatotoxicity, acyclovir was discontinued after a 10-day course of therapy. At this time serology tests for brucellosis became positive including: Wright agglutination test = 1/40, Coombs Wright = 1/80, Brucella ELISA IgG = 146.6 U/ml (normal <8 U/ml). With probable diagnosis of neurobrucellosis, triple therapy including one intravenous drug with good penetration to CSF (ceftriaxone, doxycycline and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) was started. Rifampin was avoided at this time due to abnormal liver enzymes. Within a week, the patient's symptoms including fever and psychosis improved and she became completely alert without any neurological problems and regained ability to talk and eat. Five days after discontinuation of acyclovir, serum aminotransferase levels decreased (AST = 288 IU/l and ALT = 191 IU/l) and subsequently 9 days after discontinuation of acyclovir, liver enzymes reached near-normal levels (AST = 54 IU/l and ALT = 63 IU/l). Liver biopsy also showed unremarkable portal tracts and lobules. The patient was discharged with triple oral therapy (doxycycline, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). After 3 months, she became completely well. She received 6 months' treatment totally with clinical follow-ups showing no problem at 3 months and at the end of 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old female presented with an acute 3-day history of high fever, decreased level of consciousness, hallucinations, and delusions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of high fever and altered mental status beginning 3 days prior to admission. She experienced agitation, visual hallucinations, grandiose delusions, and disorientation. On hospital day 6, she developed nausea and vomiting associated with marked acute liver enzyme elevation during empiric intravenous acyclovir therapy for suspected HSV meningoencephalitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous history of chronic febrile illness or zoonotic disease in herself or family. No history of illicit drug use; not receiving any medications prior to admission. Epidemiological history: regular consumption of unpasteurized dairy products; lived in a small town.
subjective.review_of_systems: Visual hallucinations, grandiose delusions, agitation, nausea, and vomiting. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39 °C; blood pressure, pulse rate, and respiratory rate were normal. Neurological exam: disoriented to time and place, agitated; nuchal rigidity present. Motor examination showed lower extremity muscle strength decreased to approximately 3/5, with decreased deep tendon reflexes in lower extremities. General physical examination was otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs and CSF analysis (Table 1). On hospital day 6: AST 1,093 IU/L, ALT 203 IU/L. Hepatitis and viral serologies all negative: HBsAg, anti-HCV, HAV IgM, HIV Ab, EBV VCA IgM, CMV IgM. Autoimmune liver serologies all negative: anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, liver-kidney microsomal antibody. Follow-up LFTs 5 days post-acyclovir: AST 288 IU/L, ALT 191 IU/L; 9 days post-acyclovir: AST 54 IU/L, ALT 63 IU/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT without contrast: normal. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: CSF HSV PCR negative. Brain MRI with gadolinium contrast: meningeal enhancement in left frontal and right temporal lobes, compatible with meningoencephalitis. Percutaneous liver biopsy: unremarkable portal tracts and lobules (consistent with drug-induced liver injury secondary to acyclovir).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (meningoencephalitis with acute psychotic features) and acyclovir-induced hepatotoxicity. Confirmed by positive Brucella serology: Wright agglutination test 1/40, Coombs Wright 1/80, and Brucella ELISA IgG 146.6 U/mL (normal <8 U/mL). Herpes simplex virus meningoencephalitis, viral hepatitis (A, B, C, EBV, CMV), HIV, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Empiric acyclovir was discontinued. Treated with IV ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (rifampin initially withheld due to acute hepatotoxicity). Fever and psychosis resolved within one week; patient became fully alert with normalized neurologic exam and recovered eating/speaking. Liver enzymes normalized following acyclovir cessation. Discharged on oral triple therapy (doxycycline, rifampin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) to complete a total 6-month regimen with complete recovery and no recurrence on 3- and 6-month follow-up.
